Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Making any plans for the future

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

issues.item: Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
issues.explanation: 'Irritability' is not a threat appraisal/perception item; it reflects arousal/behavioral dysregulation and fits better outside the Threat node. In this profile, the other Threat items are coherent terrorism-related hypervigilance/safety behaviors ('Scanning Exits', 'Back to Wall'), so this item is internally mismatched within the node and weakly aligned with the formulation in which Memory-linked threat should reflect perceived current danger rather than aggressive behavior.

vignette: After the bombing, Ayo’s first instinct was to distance himself from any setting that might trigger a flash of the attack. He turned to the endless scrolling of his phone, the glowing screen becoming a place where he could push aside the painful uncertainty that sat heavy in his chest. When a co‑worker suggested a new client or a quiet corner to rest, Ayo felt a sudden urge to argue, to bring the conversation into confrontation, as if the clash could drown out the dread that he could not trust his own decisions. He believed he was weak, that he could not act with certainty, and this belief pushed him toward those distractions. Because Ayo questioned his own judgment, the memories of the blast came to him in fragments that seemed alien. He could picture the bright flare of the explosion, but the faces of the people around him blurred, as if they were strangers. This emotional numbing, coupled with the sense that he did not belong in a world that seemed suddenly hostile, made it difficult for him to hold onto the details; parts of the event slipped away, leaving gaps that he could not fill. The recurring film of the subway car shaking, the smell of gunpowder, and the distant screams played on an endless loop in Ayo’s mind. Each time the image resurfaced, the urge to escape resurfaced too: he would reach for his phone, dive into a game, or ignite a quarrel with a customer in the shop. The more he tried to silence the replay, the deeper he sank into screens and conflict. With every replay, Ayo’s senses sharpened; he began to anticipate danger in the slightest movement. He learned to scan for exits whenever he stepped into a room, and he could not bring himself to sit without his back against a wall, giving him a line of sight that could reveal any threat. The memory’s vividness fueled a constant state of watchfulness that left him exhausted. The more he tried to remember, the more he felt the weight of his own inadequacy. When he found nothing to remember, he believed it proved he was a weak person, someone who could not keep his mind sharp. Each empty space in his recollection became another proof that he did not belong anywhere, reinforcing his feeling of detachment. The heightened vigilance left Ayo with no energy or desire to plan beyond the day. He avoided thinking about his future as if planning itself could create a new threat. When a client suggested a new line of work or a promotion in the shop, he would push the topic aside with an argument or an abrupt change in topic, as a way to divert the fear that lurked beneath the surface. The constant awareness of potential danger eroded his confidence. He began to doubt every decision, believing that any action might invite disaster. This erosion of trust in himself fed the belief that he was weak and that he had no place in a world that could harm him at any moment. By the time he arrived for therapy, Ayo’s tailoring shop was quiet, the racks of cloth barely moving. Customers had begun to ask why he was absent, and his own reflection in the shop window showed a man who no longer felt in control. The terror that had begun as a distant flash now dictated every step, and he feared that without help he would lose the skill that had sustained him and the sense of belonging he had once felt.
